topic_relevance.reason: The paper studies Brownian boundary limits for harmonic functions on a ball in Hardy h^p. It does not study high-threshold maxima of asymptotically Gaussian fields, moderate-deviation tails, local clumping, or cross-block exceedance control.

It provides a continuous-path baseline for defining first exit times and exit distributions, and identifies the Brownian exit law with harmonic measure/Poisson kernel. It has no jump overshoot, exterior landing law, or nonlocal Dirichlet/balayage estimate, so it cannot prove the J03 jump-process claims.

definitions.name: Brownian first exit
definitions.statement: For Brownian motion B^x starting at x in the open ball D(0,r), τ_{x,r}=inf{t≥0:B^x_t∉D(0,r)}; by path continuity B^x_{τ_{x,r}} lies on the sphere ∂D(0,r). The paper develops measurability/existence rather than taking this identification for granted.

definitions.name: Exit distribution
definitions.statement: For the unit ball, the exit point from x has density equal to the Poisson kernel k_{0,1}(x,z) relative to normalized surface measure; for x=0 the exit point is uniform on the sphere.

theorem_cards.label: Theorem 31: existence, continuity, and tightness of Brownian first-exit times
assumptions: m≥2; x is strictly inside the open ball D(0,r); Brownian motion has continuous paths and is adapted to the paper’s right-continuous filtration.
The radial levels and error parameters satisfy the stated inequalities (1.55)–(1.59); the conclusion uses almost-uniform continuity conventions.
theorem_cards.statement: For each radius r>0 the first exit time from the open ball exists as a finite-valued stopping time. As the radius varies, the first-exit-time process is almost-uniformly continuous with an explicit exceptional-probability modulus, and the family over starting points/radii is tight.
proof_steps: Approximate the target radius from above/below by a dense set of admissible radii. Use the one-dimensional Brownian reflection bound to control the probability that the exit times differ by more than 2^{-k}.
The summable exceptional-set estimates make the monotone approximating exit times converge almost uniformly to a stopping time; path continuity places the limiting exit point on the sphere.
A modulus argument extends the estimates to all radii and gives tightness from the reflection-principle tail bound.
gaps: This construction is specific to continuous Brownian paths and the sphere-radius parametrization; it does not apply automatically to discontinuous paths or nonlocal jump exits.
The estimates use a reflection principle cited from Doob and probability conventions/results imported from Chan (2021).

theorem_cards.label: Theorem 33: Brownian exit law on a sphere
assumptions: m≥2; standard m-dimensional Brownian motion; x in the open unit ball (and radius-r scaling for the centered exit).
The first-exit-time existence result is established in Theorem 31; the displayed Poisson-kernel identity for harmonic measure is cited to Durrett (1984), not proved from scratch here.
theorem_cards.statement: For continuous boundary data f on the unit sphere, E_x[f(B_{τ_{x,1}})] = ∫_{∂D} k_{0,1}(x,z)f(z)σ(dz), where k is the Poisson kernel. Starting at the center, the exit point has uniform distribution on the sphere (and radius-r exit scales to the radius-r uniform law).
proof_steps: For the Poisson-kernel identity, the author explicitly cites Durrett (1984), assertion (1), §1.10; this source does not reprove that classical identity.

For centered exit, rotational invariance of Brownian motion implies the exit distribution is rotation invariant; Corollary 14 identifies the unique rotation-invariant probability measure on the sphere as normalized surface measure.
gaps: This is a diffusion exit law supported on the geometric boundary because Brownian paths are continuous. It does not address nonlocal jump exits, where the landing point may lie anywhere in D^c.
The Poisson-kernel identity is imported from Durrett; only the rotation-invariance argument for centered exit is supplied here.

theorem_cards.label: Theorem 38: martingale maximal small-increment criterion
assumptions: Finite discrete-time martingale Z_0,…,Z_n; ε>0; the displayed special convex function λ(v)=e^{−|v|}−1+|v| and its source-specific hypothesis (1.85).
theorem_cards.statement: If Eλ(Z_n)−Eλ(Z_0) < ε^3 exp(−3ε(E|Z_0|∨E|Z_n|))/6, then P(max_{k≤n}|Z_k−Z_0|>ε)<ε.
proof_steps: The paper checks that λ meets the conditions of the maximal inequality in Bishop (1967), Chapter 8, then cites that result as Theorem 38; it does not reproduce Bishop's proof.
gaps: This is a cited martingale inequality and depends on the exact exponential convexity increment condition; it is not a generic Doob bound with arbitrary constants.

theorem_cards.label: Theorem 41: Brownian boundary limit for Hardy h^p
assumptions: Dimension m≥2, p≥1 fixed, u∈h^p harmonic on the unit ball; by Lyapunov reduction the paper assumes u(0)=0 and treats h=h^1.
Both I_{1,r}=∫|u(rz)|dσ and I_{2,r}=∫e^{−|u(rz)|}dσ converge as r↑1, with explicit rates δ_1(ε), δ_2(ε) as in (2.4)–(2.5).
The argument uses Brownian exit times, the a.u.-continuous martingale u(B_{τ_r}), and Theorem 38; statements are with the paper's constructive-probability conventions.
theorem_cards.statement: There is an increasing sequence r_q↑1 and a random variable V such that, for each q, outside a measurable set A_q of probability <2^{−q+4}, sup_{s∈[τ_{r_q},τ_1)}|V−u(B_s)|≤2^{−q+3}. Hence u(B_s)→V almost uniformly as s↑1.
proof_steps: Set λ(v)=e^{−|v|}−1+|v|; convexity plus the martingale u(B_{τ_r}) makes I_{3,r}=Eλ(u(B_{τ_r})) nondecreasing, and the two boundary-limit assumptions give I_{3,r}→b_2−1+b_1 with explicit error δ_3.
Choose r_q from δ_3 and a Brownian exit-time tail cutoff N_{2,q}, so the probability of τ_1 exceeding the time cutoff is ≤2^{−q+1}.
Partition [0,N_{2,q}] into sufficiently short intervals using Brownian almost-uniform continuity and a modulus of continuity for u on the compact ball of radius r_{q+1}.

Clip the stopped Brownian path between τ_{r_q} and τ_{r_{q+1}} at the partition times; this is a finite martingale. The increment of Eλ is bounded by the boundary error, so Theorem 38 controls the maximum deviation from the starting value except on a small set.
Combine the Brownian continuity exceptional set, exit-time tail, and martingale maximal exceptional set to get a uniform bound for every s in [τ_{r_q},τ_{r_{q+1}}].
Union the exceptional sets over k≥q; the resulting summable geometric oscillation bound makes u(B_{τ_{r_q}}) almost-uniformly Cauchy, defining V, and extends the estimate over all s∈[τ_{r_q},τ_1).
gaps: The paper's nontangential boundary limit is only a conjecture in the stated constructive setting; Theorem 43 is the classical a.e. nontangential statement, while its constructive status remains open/conjectural.
The proof relies on Brownian/harmonic structure and cannot be transferred to discontinuous jump paths without new arguments.
The Brownian martingale maximal theorem is cited to Bishop (1967), and the Poisson kernel exit identity to Durrett (1984); full proofs of those external results are not included.

constant_dependence: Theorem 41's exceptional probabilities depend explicitly on q and the convergence moduli δ_1,δ_2 through r_q; the chosen subsequence is data-dependent.
Theorem 38 carries the displayed numerical constants 1/6 and 3 from its source-specific condition; they are not asserted optimal.
endpoint_limits: Theorem 41 covers all p≥1 under both boundary-integral convergence assumptions; the non-tangential limit theorem is not established constructively by this paper.
reusable_methods: Use rotational invariance to identify the centered Brownian exit law with normalized surface measure, after proving existence and measurability of exit time/point.

To obtain an almost-uniform boundary limit, prove summable exceptional-set bounds on a sequence of stopping radii and control the path between radii via a martingale maximal criterion plus path continuity.
unchecked: External references (Bishop 1967, Durrett 1984, Helms 1969) are cited but not independently read in this card.

The article uses constructive analysis conventions for measurability, a.u. convergence, and stopping-time values; this evidence card reports its own framework rather than translating all notions to a different probability convention.
This source is only J03 adjacent background: no Lévy/jump kernel, nonlocal Dirichlet data on all D^c, overshoot, or jump-balayage formula is provided.
